Forgive
for-GIV
v.
From Old English forgiefan, “to give utterly, give up,” from for- (intensive) + giefan (give). Renders the Greek aphiēmi, “to let go, send away,” and charizomai, “to give graciously”; and the Hebrew sālach, “to forgive,” and nāsā, “to lift, bear away.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To forgive is to remit a debt that is truly owed—to release the offender from the just demand of the offence, not by pretending it did not happen, not by minimizing its weight, but by absorbing its cost in oneself and refusing to exact it from the one who owed it. The biblical word-pictures are vivid: aphiēmi sends the sin away, dismisses it, lets it go; charizomai gives graciously, treating the offence as the occasion of a free gift; the Hebrew nāsā lifts and bears the sin so that it no longer presses upon the offender; sālach is the verb God uses of His own pardon of His people. All these turn on the same reality: a real debt, a real cost, a real release. Forgiveness is therefore costly, not cheap; it is grace, not mere niceness. The cross stands at the center of the Christian doctrine of forgiveness, because there alone God forgives sin without compromise of justice: the debt is fully paid in the substitutionary suffering of His Son, so that He may be just and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus. From that fountain the believer is to forgive: forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you. The horizontal forgiveness commanded of the saint is patterned on the vertical forgiveness received—costly, free, full, and unaccompanied by the secret bookkeeping of resentment. Christ’s warning is grave: if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. Not that forgiveness earns forgiveness, but that the heart which has been truly forgiven cannot remain unforgiving; the parable of the unmerciful servant has only one ending. Forgiveness in Scripture is therefore neither cheap (it costs the cross) nor optional (it is the very air of the kingdom)—and the church which forgives as her Lord forgives is the truest credential the gospel ever sets before the watching world.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines FORGIVE as to pardon; to remit, as an offence or debt; to overlook an offence, and treat the offender as not guilty.

expand to see more

FORGIVE, v.t. — 1. To pardon; to remit, as an offence or debt; to overlook an offence, and treat the offender as not guilty. 2. To remit; as, to forgive a debt. The original sense is to give back; hence to give up the demand against an offender.

FORGIVENESS, n. — The act of forgiving; the pardon of an offender; remission of an offence, debt, or penalty; disposition to pardon; willingness to forgive.

📖 Key Scripture

Ephesians 4:32 — "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you."

Matthew 6:14-15 — "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses."

Colossians 3:13 — "Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye."

Psalm 32:1 — "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Forgiveness is corrupted, on one side, by the therapeutic version that detaches it from repentance and from the cross and reduces it to a self-help technique for the forgiver’s emotional wellbeing; and on the other, by the bitter refusal to forgive that hoards offences and forgets the parable of the unmerciful servant.

expand to see more

Therapeutic culture has rewritten forgiveness as a unilateral, self-directed exercise: forgive for your own sake, so that you can move on, so that the offender no longer occupies space in your head; forgiveness as emotional hygiene rather than as the release of a real debt; forgiveness divorced from any reckoning of justice, any call to repentance, any reference to the cross at which alone the unfathomable debt of human sin was actually paid. The result is a thinned, self-referential forgiveness that costs the forgiver nothing in particular and bears no resemblance to the costly, Christ-patterned, debt-absorbing release the New Testament commands. Recover the cross at the center, and forgiveness recovers its substance: a real debt, a real cost, a real release, given because we ourselves have been given vastly more.

The opposite corruption is the refusal to forgive that hoards offences in the heart, replays them at length, withholds reconciliation when reconciliation is offered, and lives in the slow poison of unforgiveness. Scripture is severe with this temper. The parable of the unmerciful servant says without softening that the forgiven slave who would not forgive his fellow was delivered to the tormentors; so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses. The unforgiving heart is incompatible with the kingdom of the forgiven. Where there is true repentance from the offender, forgiveness is to be extended fully; where there is not, the saint is still to lay down resentment, to commit the cause to God who judges righteously, to bless and not curse, to do good to them that hate, and to leave room for the wrath that is His and not ours. Between cheap forgiveness and bitter unforgiveness lies the costly, cross-shaped forgiveness of the Christian: full, free, debt-absorbing, patterned on the Father’s own pardon of His enemies through the blood of His Son.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aphiēmi (to let go, send away) and charizomai (to give graciously); Hebrew sālach (forgive, used only of God) and nāsā (to lift, bear away).

expand to see more

Greek aphiēmi (G863) — to send away, let go, release, remit; the main NT verb for forgiveness.

Greek charizomai (G5483) — to give freely, to forgive graciously—forgiveness as the giving of a gift.

Hebrew sālach (H5545) — to pardon, forgive—used in the OT only of God’s pardon.

Hebrew nāsā (H5375) — to lift, bear away (sin)—the verb behind the imagery of removing transgression.
